newsitem.title: GERMANY: TENNIS-LAWYERS LIKEN GRAF FATHER TO LOST, LONELY CLIMBER.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-LAWYERS LIKEN GRAF FATHER TO LOST, LONELY CLIMBER.

text.p: Lawyers for tennis star Steffi Graf's father, on trial for tax evasion, likened him on Friday to a helpless novice climber left dangling on a mountain face by advisers and tax authorities.

In their final statement as the five-month trial draws to a close, Graf's lawyers did not deny that he set out to evade up to six million marks ($3.7 million) of tax on his daughter's earnings -- less than a third of the amount claimed by the prosecution.

But they said he was a weak and vulnerable man who had been easily led astray, and that tax authorities could and should have put an end to his trangressions no later than 1992, before they became more serious.
"We're not seeking salvation by trying to reduce the sum of the tax debt," said celebrity lawyer Franz Salditt. "We don't deny the intent, but we want the background to be taken into account...
"Prominent experts led Peter Graf, the amateur, onto the tax equivalent of the north face of the Eiger and then, as he was hanging there, abandoned him," he said.

If the authorities had acted on their first suspicions, the climb would have been stopped, he said, accusing above all the regional finance ministry in Graf's home state of Baden-Wuerttemberg of turning a blind eye to avoid a scandal.
The prosecution has demanded a sentence of six years and nine months for Graf, 58, and four years and nine months for his former tax adviser Joachim Eckardt.
Steffi Graf herself, whose career earnings are estimated at more than 100 million marks ($60 million), says she handed all her financial affairs over to her father from an early age.
She is still under investigation and may face a fine after a verdict is pronounced on her father next Friday.
The final of the Australian Open in which Graf is competing in Melbourne is due to start next Friday just hours after the court verdict is announced in Mannheim.
In 1989 she faced the trauma of a highly publicised affair between her father and a call girl.
Salditt said it was this incident which triggered in Peter Graf a self-destructive slide into depression and drink.
"Peter Graf was no cold-blooded criminal, but a helpless and perplexed human being...He didn't understand tax law, but thought he did. Basically, he was a lonely man."
